speaker: Maria
words: Okay. So my name is Maria Truglio. Today is April 4th, 2022. And today, I am speaking with Mrs. Helen Lowry of Bellefonte, Pennsylvania for the Centre County, otherwise, Oral History Project. So thank you, Helen, for talking with me today. Um, the first question I wanted to ask you is, where were you living before you came to Centre County?

speaker: Helen
words: We were living in Dickinson, North Dakota. Um, we had lived in North Dakota for 14 years. Because our youngest daughter and her three, our three grandchildren live there. So we wanted to be part of their life also.

speaker: Maria
words: And how would you describe your life before coming to Centre County? For you, what were the most important aspects of your life before coming here?

speaker: Helen
words: Our life has always been very family-oriented. Um, I am the baby of 10. And we were just a tight Italian family from day one, from the minute I was born, since I was the baby. And my husband is not Italian. He was raised by grandparents. So his life was completely different than mine. But he absolutely loved my life, and kind of took it over as his. He used to tell people that my mom and dad were his. So, um, we just, we've been very lucky in our life. He's 84 and I'm 80. And we've had a wonderful life. Family has always been number one. That's how we go.

speaker: Maria
words: What is your husband's name, Helen?

speaker: Helen
words: My husband's name is Lonnie, L-O-N-N-I-E.

speaker: Maria
words: Lonnie. Okay.

speaker: Helen
words: And my middle, my main name, my maiden name, excuse me, was Melchiorre, M as in Mary, E-L-C-H-I-O-R-R-E.

speaker: Maria
words: I think that is traditionally one of the names of one of the three kings.

speaker: Helen
words: It sure is. Yes, that's what we loved to tease my father about. Are we related to them? Obviously, we weren't.

speaker: Maria
words: And Helen, were both your father and your mother of Italian origin?

speaker: Helen
words: Yes, but my mother was born in the United States. Her mom, my grandmother, which is the only grandparent we ever knew, was my mom's mom, um, she was one of 17 children. And she was born in Italy, my grandmother. And she came to America when she was 19, I think it was. And then she had eight children in the United States. My mother being one of them.

speaker: Maria
words: So your mom's mom was born in Italy, and she was one of 17 children.

speaker: Helen
words: Yes.

speaker: Maria
words: She came to the United States and then she had eight children?

speaker: Helen
words: Yeah.

speaker: Maria
words: One of whom was your mom. Okay. And tell us, um, could you tell us about your dad a little bit?

speaker: Helen
words: Yes. My dad was a wonderful person. He was not your typical Italian. He didn't have a temper. He was proud of his nationality. He was proud of his family. We lived in a community, um-. We were about five miles from Valley Forge, if anyone knows where Valley Forge is. That's where we grew up, um. And it a -, it was owned, the town was pretty much owned by Warner Company, which was a lime company there. But they also unbelievably had a, a branch here in Bellefonte. But theirs was -, they went into the ground. They, they were in tunnels like my father was in that. But most of our town was Italian. That was the, the heaviest. And then there were Spanish, we had Polish, we had German, we had Black. It was just a wonderful community. And my, my parents never drove, never had a car. And my father was the town barber in our home. So when he came home at 3:30 in the afternoon from Warner Company, he put on his white shirt and his necktie, and he became the, the barber. And he would stay open till 10:30, 11:00 because there were a lot of farmers in our area. And he would, especially, in this, you know, in this fall and the summer, wait for them to finish their work to come for a haircut. Because in those days, men got their hair cut frequently. They didn't have the long hair and all that. So, it was just a wonderful. And then, of -, the door to the barber inside was opened right into our dining room. So if we were having dinner and when it, somebody came in for a haircut, they would walk right into the house, you know, and come into the kitchen, and it was just a family -- everybody was a family.

speaker: Maria
words: And so with those people coming into your home, to have your dad cut their hair, and you were a child at this time, right, you felt safe and comfortable with the folks coming in and out?

speaker: Helen
words: Our barber shop was big, very large. We had our ironing board was set up there at all times. Because Monday, when you came home from school, it was ironing day. So, we would iron Monday after we came home. My mom had her sewing machine in there. I mean, we, it was just another room to us. And if there were no kids in there, some of the customers were like, "Pete, where's all your kids?", you know. So I mean, they were used to being part of it. And my father and mother made pizzelles, which are an Italian cookie. And they made them constantly because my father loved them. And they gave them to all his customers at Christmas time. They would have pizzelles ready for them to take home. And they would also have a drink of wine or some -- I mean, it was, it was a social as well as getting a haircut. And it was just, just a wonderful life. Just a wonderful life.

speaker: Maria
words: And this is what your father did as the sort of second shift--

speaker: Helen
words: Right.

speaker: Maria
words: -- after his daytime job. And did I understand, was that, did he go into the mines? Was it a mining kind of a job?

speaker: Helen
words: (unitelligible) He became a -- oh shoot, I forget what he became. He, he was a tinsmith for the company, for Warner Company. So he fixed any of the equipment. He made things out of tin that were little pieces leftover. You know, he made this little banks and he made -- I have a basket that I use still to this day that we used to put apples in it, but now I have clothespins in it.

speaker: Maria
words: And your dad made that?

speaker: Helen
words: My dad made it, yes. And we ha-, I have a trunk upstairs that he came -, took from Italy when he came. And he, we also had chickens, always. We always had chickens. He had a garden. We had fruit trees. And we had grapes. Of course, we always had grapes. And I don't remember it, but there's pictures of me like when I was three and four years old, we had pigs also. But I don't remember the pigs.

speaker: Maria
words: Right.

speaker: Helen
words: And um, but my mother, because my father worked all those hours, my mother was the keeper of everything, except the garden. My father did the garden. But every Saturday, this, we killed chickens, my mother, and whenever kids were around, and we, she would cut their throat and we would have them. We used to throw them and let them dance. I mean, not pleasant today, but that's what we did. And then, she had hot water. We would pick the feathers off and she would cook them on Sunday with her homemade spaghetti. So that was our dinner. And they were just hard working, too hard. They were married 67 years.

speaker: Maria
words: Wow.

speaker: Helen
words: And when my dad died, he was 87 and my mom was 93. And she lived with my -- they both lived with us because when we came, before we went to North Dakota, we had bought a house up the street from them. And then when my father couldn't do the barbering anymore and everything, they sold it and came up and lived us for-. My mom lived with us 14 years. And we just loved it. So, we had a, we really had a -- I mean, there was a lot of hardships in our life because with that amount of people. I have one sister who had a son that died at six years old from spinal meningitis.

speaker: Maria
words: I'm sorry.

speaker: Helen
words: Yeah, I mean. And we had, we had a lot of sadness, but we also had happiness. And it was my mom's family, they were all from Philly. Philadelphia.

speaker: Maria
words: Philadelphia.

speaker: Helen
words: Except my mom. She was the only one that moved to the country. And um, her father used to live in the country. They all lived there originally, but then he died and they moved in, back into the city. So, on Sundays, we could have 40 people in our house. No one was invited, you just showed up. And it was like her sister and brother-in-law would come from Philly and they would bring home water. They brought, because we had spring water in Cedar Hollow, unlike the Schuylkill River that they were drinking. So they would fill bot-, eh, big jugs of water. And my mother fed all of them. And she just, she was a hard worker. She baked on Saturday, she made pies and bread and everything. Because she didn't know what brothers or sisters were coming or what kids were coming, or grandchildren. She wanted to have enough food for everybody. And that was every, basically every Saturday and Sunday.

speaker: Maria
words: So this was not just, you know, Thanksgiving or Christmas.

speaker: Helen
words: Oh, no, no.

speaker: Maria
words: This could be any weekend, you would have that many people.

speaker: Helen
words: Yes.

speaker: Maria
words: Wow.

speaker: Helen
words: Yes, and we, most of my brothers and sisters lived, we lived within a 10-mile radius, most of us. A few moved as the years went on.

speaker: Maria
words: Right.

speaker: Helen
words: So on Saturday night, my parents loved to play poker. And it would be whoever showed up. And New Year's Eve, my husband and I probably only went out New Year's Eve maybe six times. We went to my mom and dad's house every New Year's Eve to spend it with them and play cards. And again, whatever brother and sister-in-law weren't going out, they'd show up and you just never knew how many or who. And that was, that was how our life was. And we loved it.

speaker: Maria
words: Wow. That's, you know, an amazing image to, to envision, all those folks around the table.

speaker: Helen
words: Yeah.

speaker: Maria
words: Do you happen to know where, what part of Italy your dad and your grandmother were from?

speaker: Helen
words: My dad was from Gessopalena, which is, I wrote this down, um. I thought I wrote it down, anyway. But it's like on the west side of Italy and a little bit north.

speaker: Maria
words: And a little bit more--

speaker: Helen
words: A small little town. It is still there. It's still a town there. And, um, his, his dad was also born there. He was born in 1857. And his dad died in 1943. And--

speaker: Maria
words: And was he in Italy? Did he stay in Italy?

speaker: Helen
words: Never left Italy, um. He had, he had one, he was married and had a daughter. And then that girl d-, the mother died. And then he remarried again and had three sons and that's where my father came in, the three sons.

speaker: Maria
words: Got you.

speaker: Helen
words: And then, um, his father in Italy, he, he, um, he was a tinsmith and he also, but he had grapes. And it was the typical Italian family also, um. He had o-, he had olive trees also. But, um. So he died in 1943. And I can remember my father getting a letter from Italy, saying that his father died. Because my father never went back. Once he left Italy, he never went back. And then when I was in ninth grade, this was interesting, when I was in ninth grade, my father brought one of his nephews to America. He was married and had two children, but the nephew himself had to come first. And he had to have a, a job and he lived with us. And it was the first relative of my dad's that we ever met. Because we never saw any of them.

speaker: Maria
words: So when your dad left Italy, he left behind his dad and his siblings as well--

speaker: Helen
words: Brothers, yeah.

speaker: Maria
words: -- and came alone as a young man to America.

speaker: Helen
words: Yes. And he, he ended up in Philly. He came in to, um, New York, on the ship. And then he had friends in Philly, so he took the train to Philly. And he didn't like it. And, um, my, my mother and father was very active still in the Malvern area with farming and that type of stuff, cattle. So, my father learned to be a tinsmith in Philly and a barber in Philly. And then went out to the country, which is what they call it, where we were, because it was country. And he, he worked there and then finally got a job. But he never gave up the barbering. He always did the barbering, because it was an enjoyment for him, too. He was open seven days a week. 		MT>> Wow.

speaker: Helen
words: So the, the farmers, they could work till 10:00 and they knew if they showed up at night, 10:00, my father would cut their hair. And, uh, so he just loved America. And when his nephew came, he was so proud to be able to show him Philadelphia. I mean, my father never went to the beach or anything like that. His vacation in the summer, they got a week vacation, and my father would take the train from Paoli, Pennsylvania to Philly. He would go to Horn & Hardart's, which was an old restaurant back in the day where you, you, you got your food out of these little compartments. And he would buy his barbering supplies that he would need. He might go to a movie. He would take one child with him each time he went. And I was so excited when I was picked. I was like 10 years old. And I went to Philly with my dad. I mean, it was so exciting. And then he would come home and he would be home by 3:30 because he had to open the barber shop.

speaker: Maria
words: Right.

speaker: Helen
words: So that was his one-day vacation.

speaker: Maria
words: Wow. Wow. How wonderful that you remember that, that day.

speaker: Helen
words: Yeah, yeah. It was just really special because that was what he did once a year.

speaker: Maria
words: Right.

speaker: Helen
words: That was his main day, this vacation day. And in the community, um, there w-, we had a little, um, well, we, we found out in later years that it was the Republican Club, but they didn't call it that then. And, um, the company that he worked for, Warner Company, they would have a turkey raffle, they would have Santa Claus. They would bring in somebody in the winter to do show movies. So they tried to keep their employees' children occupied, somehow, at least two or three times a year. Weddings were held there, whenever there was a wedding. They had bocce which Italian men play all the time. So that was always open Saturday and Sunday for the men. I mean, the wives and the kids weren't allowed to go there, but, um -.

speaker: Maria
words: So, it really, it was exclusively for the men. The wives and the, and the children would not attend--

speaker: Helen
words: On Saturdays and Sundays, yeah. They didn't play bocce or walk into a bar. Oh, no, no, no, no.

speaker: Maria
words: And was it for, it was that also exclusively exclusively for the Italian community? Or it was, it was open to all the group?

speaker: Helen
words: --the whole community. The whole community, yes. There were weddings there. In fact, my one sister was the last one to get married there. She got married in June of '56 and then they closed it and actually tore it down in about, uh, '58.

speaker: Helen
words: Right, yeah. So, it was just a one -- and they had live turkeys when they had the turkey thing. It was live. So you took home a live turkey in a bag and then you had to kill it and have it for Thanksgiving.

speaker: Maria
words: But your mom and dad, tha-, they did that all the time with their chickens.

speaker: Helen
words: And everybody else in town, too, did the same thing. I mean, every-, you know, all of the Italians had their own gardens and, and everything. So, it was, it was just a wonderful community to live in.

speaker: Maria
words: And do you recall about in terms of language? Do you remember anyone in your home speaking Italian or speaking a dialect? Or were they, it was everyone pretty much always speaking English?

speaker: Helen
words: No. They spoke Italian. A lot, a lot of the women came to United States later than my dad did. Or their husbands would be working at Warner Company for one or two years, and then bring them to America. So, some of the women in town never really knew how to speak English. In fact, one of my best girlfriends, from there, her mother, to the day she died, I could not understand a complete sentence that she would say to me. And different parts of Italy, as you know, talk different language.

speaker: Maria
words: Right.

speaker: Helen
words: So, they would tease each other, the men, you know, like you're talking, I don't know your language. You don't talk Italian. Of course, they were saying it in Italian. But none of the kids learned to speak Italian. Because especially in our house, my father wanted you to be an American. That's why he came. He wanted you to have a better life. With eh, he wanted his kids, if he had kids, to have a better life, he thought. So we were never taught Italian. Um, nut on Sundays, when my mother's family would come and they would all sit around and they talked complete Italian so that we knew nothing, and it was, it was always fun because we would all try to, "What are they saying? Let's try and figure out what they're saying." But that, it was, yeah, so they all used two languages. And then, and then you had the Germans that were there that spoke their language. The Polish had a little language. So it was, it was a well-molded family area. All the, all the men worked at the same place. And the women all stayed home. And then during the War, World War II, the women, my mother included, she got a job at a -. It was called Bishops and they were making stuff for the service. I forget what they were making now, but they made stuff. And the women worked night shifts.

speaker: Maria
words: Right. Wow.

speaker: Helen
words: And then, come home and then do their day, day work as a wife and mother.

speaker: Maria
words: In fact, you mentioned that your dad got news of his father's passing in 1943.

speaker: Helen
words: Yes.

speaker: Maria
words: Which, which made me, you know, think of the period of World War II. Do you, do you remember, did you perceive what your dad's feelings were about the war? Because at that point, the United States was at war against Italy.

speaker: Helen
words: Right. Well, first of all, my mother only -- let me throw this out. My mother only went to third grade. And then she had to quit school to work for her father and mother. And my father came from Italy when he was 17. So he learned English and American reading. That's what he was trying to learn. And I, I don't remember this, but my brother who's closest to me remembered and he told me about this. When dad got his letter, my father couldn't read the letter. It was written all in Italian. And he went next door and the man next door read it to him that his father had died. And it was, it was just, I mean, my father was very tight with his family, but his family wasn't his family. Italy was not his family anymore. And my father was a very soft-hearted person. He cried. He cried at everything. He was very sentimental. Whenever the girls got married, he cried. Before we even got to the church, he was crying. And it wasn't like we were going anyplace. My husband and I lived with them for two years after we got married. But, um, my father was just -- and that's true with a lot of Italian men, which people don't realize. They are very, um, easy-hearted for their family and their wives and children and, um, tears come easy to them. But that's a side that you don't hear or see.

speaker: Maria
words: In the stereo-, in the stereotypes that we get in movies and TV,-- 		HL>> Right.

speaker: Maria
words: --they don't show that aspect. Yeah, yeah.

speaker: Helen
words: Right. And they're short. Italian men are usually short. They're, they're not over -- I don't know any of them that we're related to that were over, nobody was 6 feet.

speaker: Maria
words: Right, right.

speaker: Helen
words: Nobody.

speaker: Maria
words: The same in my family as well with the men, yeah. Not, not very tall.

speaker: Helen
words: Yes.

speaker: Maria
words: So Helen, then, when was it -- so, so you grew up in this area near Valley Forge, you said. Then you were in North Carolina?

speaker: Helen
words: North Dakota.

speaker: Maria
words: North Dakota, I'm sorry.

speaker: Helen
words: Big difference.

speaker: Maria
words: Yes.

speaker: Helen
words: Big difference. Excuse me. It just reminded me of something. There, it's all Norwegian and Swedes in North Dakota. That's the nationality is, period.

speaker: Maria
words: Wow.

speaker: Helen
words: And we lived, we moved to -- the first place we moved to was Williston, North Dakota, which is in the northwest corner, almost in Montana, and almost in Canada. Everybody was blonde and light-skinned, okay. And my best friend there, that I'm still friends with today, she would introduce me as, "This is Helen, my friend. She's Italian. And she just moved here from Pennsylvania." I mean, I was like this, "This -, oh, this is a joke." And, it was just funny. I mean, that's how they identified me. I was, I was the only Italian in town.

speaker: Maria
words: You were "the Italian.

speaker: Helen
words: I was the Italian. Italian, yeah.

speaker: Maria
words: And did you feel then in that community, I mean, it sounds like you remember very clearly that you stood out for that reason. But did you feel any, um, negativity towards you because of that? Or was it more welcoming, or?

speaker: Helen
words: It was more interesting, um. A lot of them never really had real spaghetti or gravy that you -- well, we called it gravy, that's what we call it -- that you make from scratch. And, um, pizzelles, which we always made. My husband always makes them. So, the Italian food was entirely different to them. And they all started to love it, my f-, our friends and who we met, um, and they--

speaker: Maria
words: When you, when you cooked for them, they would love it?

speaker: Helen
words: Yes. And, um, I'd, I'd invite them up and we would have a dinner. And just, it was just wonderful. I mean, it was just that. In fact, one time, I mean I was with -- I always had dark hair, of course, and dark skin. And I always stood out then in North Dakota because of that. And I went to Minot, which is a big town. It's an, an army base is there also. It's a very big town. We, the government has a nice base there. But they had the Swedish festival every fall. And they came from Sweden and Norway to participate in this. And I went on a bus trip with a group of people. And I said to the girl sitting next to me, I said, "You do realize that this is not the true United States in this state. Do you realize that?" And she said, "What do you mean?" I said, "Well, you don't have Italians, you don't have Mexicans, you don't have Black." I mean, it was just white blonde women and men. And that was just such a joke. She said, "Oh, I never thought of it like that." She said, "Well, when we get to Minot tonight, when the sailers, or the soldiers come in, you'll see all of that. They, they'll bring it up with them." And that was their only exposure to Black, Mexican, Italians, German, all of that. It was, it was just a whole different life.

speaker: Maria
words: So yeah, because you grew up in such a diverse community and tight-knit community. So that was a huge difference.

speaker: Helen
words: Yes.

speaker: Maria
words: So, Helen, how did you feel? So, when did you come to Bellefonte and what brought you here? And then maybe if you can also kind of compare Bellefonte to those previous two places that you had lived in.

speaker: Helen
words: Okay. We --. Our grandchildren, I don't know how, but they grew up. And we said -- And my, our daughter was living like two hours out of town on a ranch. So we weren't seeing her that frequently either. So, we decided it was time to move back to Pennsylvania because we were missing the family that was left. But my parents were gone, of course, and everything was brothers and sisters. So, we didn't want to go back to the King of Prussia area because it's just too busy for us down there, especially coming from North Dakota where, where you could walk down the street and you never had a car. So, we started looking t-, for where to go. And we couldn't find. We came in to, to Pennsylvania and looked at a few places, but we didn't see anything we liked. So we went back to North Dakota. And I was at work and I was talking to my friend who loved to play on the computer. And, and I said, "You know, Lonnie used to like to go to Bellefonte with his grandparents when he was little. They went every summer. And he had gone to the Grange Fair when he was little. So he remembered that. In fact, he took me after we were married, and I wasn't as impressed, but anyway. So, my friend said, "Well, let's see if we can find a place." And she found this just starting, this development that we're in, OpeQuon Hill. And she says, "Look at this. This is the new development going up in Bellefonte." I said, "Well, that would really be good." So, that's how we found it. And then, our granddaughter was getting married in Pennsylvania. So, when we came back for her wedding in '07, we came and looked at these. And they, um, my husband liked it because it was close for him to go to camp. And we liked the quietness. It was sort of like North Dakota, a small community, uh, the town being small, um, walkable, you know, safe. So, that's where we ended up and we love it. We love it.

speaker: Maria
words: And that was 2007 is when you--

speaker: Helen
words: Seven, yeah.

speaker: Maria
words: And, um, when you came to Bellefonte, wh- like how did you establish a new sense of community? Because it sounds like, you know, certainly you had that built in in your childhood home with everybody coming in to get their haircut.

speaker: Maria
words: You know, were there ways for you to establish a sense of community here?

speaker: Helen
words: Yes. Number one, of course, I'm Catholic and I joined Catholic Daughters, which is a great way to meet people. And I also became a volunteer at the Breast Center because I am an ovarian cancer survivor. And I wanted to be involved with the hospital, but I didn't want to work in the hospital and the Breast Center is in the building in front of the hospital. So, that worked out really well. I got to meet a lot of people there. And then I belong to an ovarian cancer group and we still do lunch. In fact, we just had lunch two weeks ago. And, um, um, our community here, our development, the people were all very friendly, and we have all different kinds and t-, shapes and ages and everything and we're twin, our houses are twins. So our neighbor next door, um, we're very close to. They lived in Bellefonte their whole life. So they have a lot of history. And, and, and as I say, my husband came here a lot when he was young, so he knows the fishing and all that. But, um, we loved it here. And we have, we have had more company here because it's easy for my nieces and nephews to come here, it's only two and a half, three-hour ride. And we have enough room where they can all stay. And, um, so we still feel the, the family, our attachment to our family. And my husband was an only child. So, it was a whole--

speaker: Maria
words: Quite a difference.

speaker: Helen
words: It was a whole life for him and he just loved my life, our life. But he thought I had a great life.

speaker: Maria
words: Right, right. So Helen, in the time you've been here in, in Bellefonte and, and Centre County, um, have you experienced either yourself or, do y-, you know, have you witnessed any sort of what you would call racism in the community? You spoke a little bit about how in North Dakota, you were the Italian, you know, of-. Anything that you would, like in a negative sense, perceive is racism?

speaker: Helen
words: No, never. In fact, a couple in our development, they were the first people we met and, um, they're a, um, mixed couple. And he is wonderful, and just wonderful people. And I don't say that I don't -- to me anyway, skin color and that type of thing, that doesn't matter. I mean, it's, it's what comes out of your mouth and who you are that is important to me. I don't care what you look like or what you do when you walk in your house and the door shut. That's not my problem. But when you're kind and friendly out front, that's, that's what I love.

speaker: Maria
words: And so, it sounds like you've got a, another home where you feel a strong sense of community and closeness in the family and, and beyond the family.

speaker: Helen
words: Yes, yeah.

speaker: Maria
words: Do you feel like since you arrived in 2007, and now it's 2022, um, do you feel like you've seen changes in Centre County, for, for better or for worse or just neutral? You know, in what, in what ways do you see the county changing over time?

speaker: Helen
words: Well, of course, the growth. Before even, I mean, Bellefonte, especially. Um, you -. When we first came, you could ride to Bellefonte and you might see -- at night, I'm talking about after 7 -- you might see five or six cars, or past five or six cars. But now, there's traffic all the time. You can see there's a lot more people, a lot more cars parked along the streets in Bellefonte at night, um. And I think that's good, because it's, it's a variety, um. And of course, also with that does come some outside problems. But I always feel if you just live your life, no, especially at my age, you're not running the streets at, at 8:00 at night at our age, you know. We're one of those that eats at 4:30, 5:00 and then we're done for the night, but. So if we go out to dinner, it's, you know, early. But, uh.
